newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinian police try to prevent clashes.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian police try to prevent clashes.

text.p: Palestinian police tried to keep a lid on protests in the West Bank and Gaza on Saturday as the United States worked frantically to arrange an Israeli-PLO summit to end violence threatening Middle East peace.

Palestinian police in riot gear prevented hundreds of youths from marching on an Israeli checkpoint at Ramallah, north of Jerusalem, scene of some of the fiercest fighting in the past four days which has claimed nearly 70 lives.
But Palestinian stone-throwers clashed with soldiers in areas still occupied by Israel, witnesses said.

U.S. diplomats rushed to Gaza on Saturday to urge Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to meet Israel's right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose decision to open a tunnel near Moslem shrines in Jerusalem ignited the violence.
Diplomatic sources said Netanyahu had rejected an Egyptian offer to host the summit in Cairo. Arafat has turned down a bilateral meeting with Netanyahu, they said.
Arafat is insisting that Netanyahu close the tunnel before a meeting, the sources said.
"There is no meeting planned for tonight," Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters, dismissing widespread speculation that a U.S.-brokered summit was imminent.
"Our demands are clear. We want them to close the tunnel, put the peace process back on track, and immediately implement the Oslo accords," he said.

Netanyahu's reluctance to implement the Oslo self-rule agreement, which includes a partial Israeli troop withdrawal in Hebron, fuelled the Palestinian suspicion and frustration which boiled over when he opened the tunnel beside the al-Aqsa and Dome of the Rock mosques.

Since the violence erupted on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and his Middle East coordinator Dennis Ross have made dozens of phone calls to Netanyahu, Arafat, Mubarak and other key leaders.
"The Israelis want a bilateral meeting, we welcome a three-way meeting in Cairo and the Americans are working hard to convene a meeting attended by either Christopher or Ross," Abu Rdainah added.
Arafat said the meeting would take place but did not specify a time.
"I will meet him (Netanyahu) in Cairo," Arafat told reporters in self-ruled Gaza.
Arafat has ordered his 30,000-strong paramilitary force to rein in demonstrators and not to shoot at Israelis unless fired upon.

Youths clashed, however, for a fourth straight day with Israeli troops. Soldiers fired rubber bullets and threw percussion grenades at stone-throwers at Kalandia refugee camp between Jerusalem and Ramallah.
In the villages of Halhoul and Beit Umar near Hebron soldiers fired teargas and rubber bullets at Palestinians who burned tyres and blocked roads.

In Jerusalem, Palestinian demonstrators came to the rescue of four Israeli police injured when their jeep overturned in Arab East Jerusalem while on the way to quell an Arab protest in nearby Jabal al-Mukaber village, witnesses said.
Palestinian demonstrators rushed to the soldiers, gave them water and helped them to ambulances, they added.
Israeli security forces had earlier shot and wounded three Palestinians during stone-throwing confrontations in Jabal al-Mukaber.
Palestinians in the West Bank observed a general strike to mourn the 54 victims killed in clashes since Wednesday. Fourteen Israeli soldiers have died.
Netanyahu has accused Arafat of "cynically" exploiting the tunnel issue and instigating the violence.
Palestinians called the tunnel's opening an assault on Islamic holy shrines and an Israeli attempt to "Judaise" Arab East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel in 1967 and later annexed.
"Keeping the tunnel open means pushing the whole region towards irresponsible violence," the PLO said in the statement.
The Moslem world has condemned Israel and the leaders of France, Britain and Germany have made an unprecedented joint appeal to Netanyahu and Arafat to meet.
